title: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
openingText: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it. This belief was not without its grounds. The preparations of both the combatants were in every department in the last state of perfection; and he could see the rest of the Hellenic race taking sides in the quarrel; those who delayed doing so at once having it in contemplation. Indeed this was the greatest movement yet known in history, not only of the Hellenes, but of a large part of the barbarian world—I had almost said of mankind.
about:
Thucydides invented political history. He wrote about a war he had fought in—and been exiled for losing—determined to record what actually happened rather than what people wished had happened. The result is a book without sentimentality: speeches that show how each side justified itself, a plague that dismantled Athenian society from within, a dialogue in which might-makes-right is stated without apology, and an expedition to Sicily that becomes a slow-motion catastrophe. Hobbes translated it in 1629 because he recognised his own world in it.

Modern political realists still claim Thucydides as their founding text. He believed that power follows fixed laws, that idealism gets cities destroyed, and that the strong do what they can while the weak suffer what they must. But the book is also a tragedy: Athens was the freest and most creative city in the ancient world, and Thucydides watched it destroy itself. He makes sure you feel both things at once.

angleCards.title: Speeches as politics in action.
angleCards.text: Thucydides gives each side its own voice — Athenians argue for empire, Spartans argue for stability, the Melians argue for justice. He does not say who is right. I want to read tracking how each speech reveals the inner logic of a position, not just the stated reasons.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading the History as a series of political arguments in action — tracking how Thucydides uses speeches to reveal the internal logic of each side, and what he thinks about the gap between the reasons people give and the reasons they actually act on.

angleCards.title: The Melian Dialogue and political realism.
angleCards.text: In 416 BCE, Athens sent envoys to the neutral island of Melos and told them: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Negotiate or die. I want to read the whole work as the argument that leads to this moment — and to decide whether Thucydides endorses it or mourns it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading the History to understand the Melian Dialogue — the foundational text of political realism — and to trace how Thucydides builds toward it, whether he endorses the Athenian position, and what the outcome reveals about the limits of pure power politics.

angleCards.title: The plague and the collapse of norms.
angleCards.text: In Book II, plague strikes Athens. Thucydides does not only describe the disease — he describes what it does to social behaviour, to religious belief, to the willingness to keep promises. I want to read his account as a clinical study of how crisis dissolves the moral framework of a society.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading the History for Thucydides’ plague narrative — not just as medical history but as an analysis of how catastrophe destroys social norms, what holds communities together under extreme pressure, and whether Athens ever recovered the values it lost.

angleCards.title: The Sicilian Expedition as self-destruction.
angleCards.text: Books VI–VII describe Athens sending its greatest fleet to conquer Sicily, losing it entirely, and never recovering. It is one of the most gripping strategic narratives in any language. I want to read tracking the decision-making failures — how a democracy talked itself into disaster.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading the History for the Sicilian Expedition — how Athens, at the height of its power, decided on a catastrophic overreach, why democratic deliberation failed to stop it, and what Thucydides thought the disaster revealed about the structural weaknesses of Athenian power.

cast.name: Pericles
cast.description: The dominant figure of the war’s opening years — strategist, orator, and the man who gave the Funeral Oration defining what Athens was fighting for. Thucydides regarded him as the one leader who understood the war’s real logic and how Athens could win it without overreaching.

cast.name: Cleon
cast.description: The leather-tanner who became Athens’s most powerful voice after Pericles died in the plague. Thucydides despised him — too loud, too confident, too willing to use the assembly’s anger as a weapon. His victory at Pylos is described with barely concealed irritation.

cast.name: Alcibiades
cast.description: The most brilliant and destructive figure in the war — charismatic enough to lead Athens, reckless enough to abandon it when accused of sacrilege, clever enough to survive by switching sides twice. The chief advocate for the Sicilian Expedition who did not stay to command it.

cast.name: Nicias
cast.description: The Athenian general who opposed the Sicilian Expedition on the floor of the assembly, was outvoted, and was then appointed to lead it. Pious, cautious, and unlucky, he delayed the fleet’s escape by waiting for an eclipse and was captured and executed with his army.

cast.name: Brasidas
cast.description: The most gifted Spartan general of the war — quick, persuasive, and effective in ways Sparta rarely was. He liberated northern Greek cities from Athenian rule by argument as much as force, and died at the moment of his greatest victory at Amphipolis.

cast.name: Hermocrates
cast.description: The Syracusan statesman who warned his city that Athens was coming, organised its defence, and helped destroy the greatest fleet Athens ever sent out. He understood Athenian strategy better than most Athenians did and used that knowledge to save his city.
